children: U.S. stock markets this week moved amid geopolitical developments, including a potential arrangement with Tehran and a high stakes summit with Chinese premier Xi Jinping.
All eyes were on the oil and gas markets, with reports of a potential phased arrangement between the U.S. and Iran to restore Strait of Hormuz ship traffic.
Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump also wrapped up their summit stateside, with little to show beyond a two-month extension of the existing trade truce.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields continued to rise this week as the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield
topped 5.15%, marking its strongest reading since July 2007.
Major stock indices made advancements in the week. The blue-chip Dow added +0.28%, the benchmark S&P gained +1.21%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed up +2.06%.
Here were some of the trending stocks that caught investor attention this week:
AMD

became the latest chipmaker to cross the $1 trillion mark in valuation amid a broader rally in chips and artificial intelligence companies on Monday. It follows in the footsteps of Nvidia, Broadcom, and Micron.
Novo

shares fell after its Capital Markets Day presentation in London on Monday. The company unveiled its 2030 growth targets, including a $23B obesity sales target and plans to launch more than five multi-blockbusters by 2030. Novo also aims to have at least five Phase 3 programs each in obesity/diabetes and other therapy areas while expanding oral GLP-1 capacity to serve 10 times while expanding capacity to serve 10x more people with obesity on oral GLP-1 by 2030.
Amazon
blocked Meta's

Muse from its platform as part of a ban of third-party shopping robots. This is notable as Muse's promise is to assist humans by semi-autonomously doing research, booking meetings and tickets, and making purchases on its own.
Paramount Skydance
, the Writers Guild of America, and twelve attorneys general agreed on the terms that would enable the entertainment conglomerate to complete its $111B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
. Paramount agreed to keep its headquarters in California, among other concessions in the settlement deal.
Oracle
fell Thursday after
Bloomberg

reported the company is moving to shield itself from rising expenses on its massive Project Jupiter data center being built in New Mexico, sending a notice citing force majeure to the project's developer. Oracle is trying to insulate itself from having to make payments if the 2.45 GW facility project is unable to bring capacity online in 2028 as was expected, the report said. Bloom Energy
, whose fuel cells are set to power the project, also fell.
McDonald's
announced its

at its recent investor day, committing roughly $8.5 billion to help franchisees modernize restaurants, improve operations, and enhance the customer experience. The company said it is targeting operating margins in the low-to-mid 50% range by 2030.
Micron Technology

was in focus on Wednesday as Citi upped its earnings estimates on the memory maker, citing better-than-expected pricing for dynamic random access memory. "We model F4Q26 sales/EPS of $51B/$31.45, above consensus of $50.8B/$31.43 and F1Q27 sales/EPS of $57B/$35.25, above consensus of $56.7B/$35.15," Citi analyst Atif Malik wrote in a note to clients. "We raise near-term NAND/DRAM pricing assumptions on non-SCA contracted bits."
Costco

delivered another better-than-expected quarter with a top- and bottom-line beat. Total revenue, including a 7% increase in membership fees of $1.85B (vs. $1.83B estimates), increased 12% to $95.72B, beating estimates by $830M, and contributed to a profit of $6.75 per share. The bottom line improved 15% year-over-year and was 5 cents better than expected. Comparable sales in the U.S. were up 7.2% on an adjusted basis (vs. 6.85% estimates).
